newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Metals - Chile strike not seen hitting copper.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Chile strike not seen hitting copper.

text.p: An impending strike at a small Chilean copper mine will have little impact on prices as world supply is in surplus and looks like staying that way well into 1997, Far East traders said on Wednesday.
"There won't be any flow-on impact from the strike," an industry executive in Beijing said.
"Things have been quiet for a while. We're looking at a surplus, so there is no big pressure on the market," he said.
Workers at Chilean state mining company Codelco's Salvador copper mine voted on Wednesday to begin an indefinite strike from August 31 in support of wage demands, a union leader said.
The strike would be joined by all five unions at the mine, one of Codelco's smallest, producing 42,901 tonnes of fine copper in the first half of 1996.
TheBeijing-based source said the international copper surplus could be as high as 150,000 tonnes and probably would pressure the market through 1997.
Traders said London Metal Exchange (LME) copper stocks have been and stood at 271,675 tonnes on August 23.
The 5,000-tonne rise in stocks on Friday was in line with market expectations but underlined the strong rising trend in inventory levels.
"LME stocks can be quite artifical because new stock, new production is not registered," another Asian source said.
Premiums remained high, traders said, firming again to around $165 to $170 a tonne over the LME cash price from Singapore warehouses.
"Once the stock level (in Singapore) comes back, we will see a more normal premium," a Chinese trader said.
He added: "10,000 to 15,000 (tonnes) is healthy, then you would expect the premium to be around $100.".

The market is also waiting for news from a looming labour dispute at Phelps Dodge's 170,000 tonnes a year contained copper operations at Chino in New Mexico, where the company has so far had no response to last week's final contract offer.

And Gold Field Namibia Ltd reported on Wednesday that the copper smelter at its Namibian subsidiary Tsumeb Corp Ltd (TCL) had been badly damaged by striking mineworkers and would be out of action for a long time.
TCL sold 6,789 tonnes of copper and 12,142 tonnes of lead in the quarter to end-June.
A fall in the LME price of lead to below $800 a tonne for three-month metal had not prompted Chinese sellers to shift their price levels accordingly, a trader with a Chinese firm in Hong Kong said.
LME lead finished Tuesday's trading day at $795 a tonne, a loss of $12 from Friday. The LME was closed on Monday for a public holiday.
London traders described the market as bullish on lead in the medium to long term, with one source saying it could go dowm to $780 a tonne.
"There are some offers from China at around $810, but this is higher than customers can accept," he said, adding that the Chinese offers were for LME unregistered metal.
"Chinese are slow to put their prices down," he said.
Taiwanese and South Korean customers were interested in paying lead premiums of $30 over the LME spot price, he said, but Chinese offers came with a $50-60 premium.
